source.title: Cockpit: A Practical Debugging Tool for the Training of Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Frank Schneider; Felix Dangel; Philipp Hennig

record.tranche_reason: The paper does not test the listed claim versions. Its experiments measure optimizer-related changes in the Hessian maximum eigenvalue, but do not measure training–test gaps or generalization on held-out data.
record.gate_note: The paper describes TIC as a proxy for the generalization gap, but reports no TIC result. Appendix D.2 compares SGD and GD on a synthetic regression task and reports a Hessian-eigenvalue result; that measurement does not establish an effect on the generalization gap.
record.test_reason: No result tests V1–V8. Appendix D.2 compares unscaled Hessian eigenvalues without held-out performance; it measures neither V5's batch-size accuracy penalty nor V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–generalization-gap association. Figure 5 reports test accuracy across learning rates, but tests none of the specified comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes Appendix D.2: mini-batch noise reduces late-training maximum Hessian eigenvalues despite similar loss curves, without demonstrating a generalization-gap effect. The paper's broader conclusion is that Cockpit provides useful training diagnostics at manageable computational cost.
record.recipe_differences: No experiment tests the claim’s interventions or measures its train–test gap.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer and batch size differ between SGD (|B| = 95) and GD (|B| = N = 100).

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic scalar regression, SGD with batch size 95 decreases the maximum Hessian eigenvalue during later training relative to full-batch GD, despite similar loss curves.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mini-batch noise can alter late-training curvature without an evident change in training loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Across four DeepOBS classification problems, the best learning-rate settings have positive median normalized step size; excessive overshooting gives poor test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Good learning-rate settings can overshoot local directional minima, with the preferred normalized step size depending on the problem.

record.problems: The relevant Appendix D.2 result is shown only as a figure, with no numerical values or uncertainty reported. The experiment uses synthetic regression and does not report held-out performance or a training–test gap.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label and random-label held-out performance.
Test error as width increases beyond that needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under specified tuning regimes.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus training–test gaps, including ranking against alternative measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Correct the record's blanket statement that the paper reports no held-out performance: Section 3.3 and Figure 5 report final test accuracy. Those results still do not test any listed version. TIC estimates are provided as diagnostic instruments, including in Figure 2, but their relationship to measured generalization gaps is not validated here.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and held-out performance on natural labels.
Test error across widths beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error.
Held-out performance of adaptive optimizers versus SGD.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the training–test gap.
Test-accuracy effects of removing memorized examples.
